title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 1
intro: This is your whole Bad Trips guide as it is published today (it matches the editor HTML you pasted, block for block), with my suggestions marked where they apply. Nothing changes until you approve it.

The first card is the one big question: how the quick version and the long version split the work. Most of the repetition is between the checklist, the Longer Triage and the long sections, so those cuts wait for your answer. The other cards are repeats and safety lines inside the long part, which come out whichever way you answer, and seven questions only you can answer (in six of them the guide says two things that don't fit together). Three fresh readers are reading the whole guide for this, two for repeats and one for safety lines: the cards come from my read, both repeat readers' reports and the first half of the safety reader's, and every quote on them was checked against your text.

Pangram (your extension, on the published post) reads the guide as AI overall. The full analysis didn't open from here, so there are no window readings on this page yet. Humanizing starts once the structure is settled, so no work goes into paragraphs that are about to be cut.

structure.label: Structure
structure.about: how the quick version and the long version split the guide, and where a part goes

suggestions.title: How should the quick and long versions split the work?
suggestions.question: A (my pick): the Quick Bad Trip Checklist stays at the top, but each step becomes its heading and one or two of your own lines saying what to do, with a link to its section below. Step 1 keeps its danger signs in full, since someone in an emergency shouldn't have to click. Everything else is said once, in the long part. The Longer Triage goes: its paragraphs that aren't said anywhere else (the emergency room isn't magic; the body writing the horror story; love isn't stubbornness) move to the sections they belong to. B: keep today's order (checklist, Longer Triage, outside help, medical rescue, remedies, tripsitting, the shadow-work essays) and only cut the repeats inside it, keeping the fuller copy each time. C: take the quick version out of the post, since the web app at ibogaqueen.com/1625-2/ already is one, and open the post with a short "In a crisis right now?" box: the danger signs, the brain-damage branch and the link to the app.
suggestions.why: Most of the guide's advice is told three or four times: in the checklist (15 steps), in the Longer Triage (5 questions), and again in the long sections. The brain-damage order is told six times, "I do not yet have data that pes-caprae aborts MDMA" five times, the support lines three times, and one 38-word quote ("I hear how vast and certain this feels...") twice word for word. A quick version that only points to the long part lets each thing be said once.
suggestions.stays: Whichever you pick, each checklist step keeps its heading and its first action in your words, and every paragraph that goes is listed with the place that already says it.
suggestions.advice_note: A: it keeps the quick read you want and takes out the third and fourth tellings. B leaves most of the repetition between the checklist and the long part. C makes the post depend on the web app for the quick version. With A, the next page shows the new checklist in full, step by step, for your OK.

suggestions.title: Humic acid: lick it first, or smell it first?
suggestions.question: The Core Order's first step says "Smell humic acid, take a 5mg lick of it", and Humic Acid Brings Brain to Optimal Function says a 5mg lick sends your brain "into hyperfunctionality". Some Remedies Require More Caution says eating it "can produce a hyperintelligent state", could destabilize somebody prone to mania, "I wouldn’t use it casually during a bad trip", and "I’d start with" smelling it. Which should the guide say for someone whose brain feels damaged: (a) smell it, and lick a tiny bit only if smelling doesn't help and they aren't prone to mania; (b) smell it and lick 5mg, as the Core Order says; (c) your words?
suggestions.why: A reader who follows the Core Order would do what the caution section warns against.
suggestions.stays: All three passages stay as they are until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): it fits both passages, and the lick stays available when smelling isn't enough.

suggestions.title: Where does "Hello, Lovey Bunny!" go?
suggestions.question: Your greeting, the MAPS video and the Challenging Psychedelic Experiences Project paragraph sit under Shadow Work and Tripsitting Yourself or Others, about 7,500 words into the post, where the post first began. (a) Leave them there, as the opening of the tripsitting and shadow-work half; (b) move the greeting to the very top, above the checklist; (c) your words?
suggestions.why: A reader meets the greeting after the medical chemistry, which reads like a second start.
suggestions.stays: Everything stays where it is until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): someone opening the guide in trouble needs the checklist first, and the greeting opens the half they read once they are safe.

suggestions.title: DMSO first: two cautions from the DMSO section
suggestions.question: The brain-damage branch puts DMSO first, whatever the drug. The DMSO section says "Don’t take it with drugs that should not absorb rapidly, including corticosteroids, NSAIDs, and harmalas", and ayahuasca is a harmala brew (the serotonin section says "harmala/ayahuasca-type MAOI exposure"). It also says "Don’t combine it with blood-thinning medication because DMSO also thins the blood", while the stroke paragraph uses DMSO at once though "DMSO cannot identify whether the problem is a clot, a hemorrhage". What holds for (a) someone on ayahuasca and (b) a possible bleed? If DMSO still comes first in both, the DMSO section is what changes; if not, the brain-damage branch says what to do instead. Tell me which, in your words, and I'll draft the line for your OK.
suggestions.why: A reader in that situation meets both instructions and can't follow both. Readers A and B each found this.
suggestions.stays: Everything stays as it is until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: This one is yours: only you know what you do with DMSO in these two cases.

suggestions.title: How long the action lock lasts
suggestions.question: The 3 a.m. note in checklist step 6 says "No big actions until morning." No Rash Actions says "Use a 24–72 hour action lock." and "Until you have slept and eaten, don’t drive...". (a) Leave them: the note covers the first night and the lock is the full rule; (b) make the 3 a.m. note say the same as the lock; (c) your words. (The Alone at 3 a.m. section quotes the note as "No actions until morning", without "big"; I'd make it match whichever you pick.)
suggestions.why: Readers A and B each found the three lengths, with nothing saying which applies when.
suggestions.stays: All three stay as they are until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): each fits the person reading it, and the lock section is where the full rule lives.

suggestions.title: Room first, or body first?
suggestions.question: The checklist says "Use this in order." and puts the room before the body ("fix the room, help the body, find one calm human"). Stillness or Movement?, the fear loop and the shadow-thoughts section put the body first ("body → room → human → time"). (a) Room first everywhere, as the checklist says; (b) body first everywhere; (c) leave them, if the difference is on purpose.
suggestions.why: A reader who follows the checklist and then the loop breaker gets two orders, with no reason for the change.
suggestions.stays: All four places stay as they are until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): the checklist is the order the reader is told to follow; only the word order changes in the other three.

suggestions.title: Ocean water and charcoal water: different, or alike?
suggestions.question: Ocean water's section says its effect is "different from DMSO, aged ozonated-charcoal water, zeolite, or beach morning glory". The next section opens, right under its heading, "These work similarly to ocean water." (a) Take "aged ozonated-charcoal water" out of the first list; (b) change the second to say how they differ; (c) your words.
suggestions.why: Read together, the two lines say opposite things.
suggestions.stays: Both stay as they are until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): it takes one item out of that list and keeps both sections as you wrote them.

suggestions.title: Charcoal: only after a recent oral ingestion?
suggestions.question: Checklist step 12 (stopping a trip) says "Charcoal belongs only in the separate recent-oral-ingestion branch." The gut tools use it outside that branch: "Activated charcoal can help gut toxicity, but it adsorbs drugs. Sometimes that is exactly the point.", "When the goal is to reduce drug absorption or stop a toxic gut situation, charcoal may be relevant.", and after a ferment, "which then requires activated charcoal to reduce gut histamine". (a) Limit the sentence to stopping a trip: "To stop a trip, charcoal belongs only in the separate recent-oral-ingestion branch."; (b) take that sentence out of step 12; (c) your words.
suggestions.why: A reader who follows step 12 would never use charcoal for the gut problems the long part uses it for. Readers A and B each found this.
suggestions.stays: Everything stays as it is until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (b): step 12's next paragraph and step 10 already say when charcoal fits and when it is dangerous, so nothing is lost and the contradiction goes.
